#6254. The 7 Best Electric Stoves to Upgrade Your Kitchen

These expert-picked models cook cleaner than gas, and offer features like convection and air fry.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Electric stoves burn cleaner and more efficiently than gas—in fact, per the Department of Energy, they’re about three times more energy-efficient than their gas counterparts. They’re also more straightforward to install—no gas line needed—and often feature flat, easy-to-clean, glass-ceramic cooktops. Plus, their ovens preheat quickly and provide even and consistent heat, which is ideal for anyone who loves to bake. No wonder electric stoves have become the go-to for the majority of households in the U.S.

Electric stoves and ranges come in a wide range of sizes and styles, and many models even have high-tech features such as convection baking, air frying with more room for food than countertop models, and Wi-Fi connectivity. These stoves make a great addition to any kitchen as they’re versatile, reliable, and often quite affordable, too. Plus, some even qualify for a tax rebate.

We rounded up the best of the best, so when you're ready to replace your existing electric stove—or switch from gas—you’ll know just what you need.

Frigidaire makes several lines of well-regarded electric stoves. This 30-inch freestanding model strikes a balance between affordability and modern features like air fry, standard convection, and a user-friendly mix of four stove-top control knobs and an oven touch screen. It’s also available as a slide-in version.

The spacious oven ensures even baking and roasting, with ample room between pans. It also lets you switch between standard baking and convection, making it ideal for those new to convection cooking. The built-in air fry function delivers crisp results without excess oil, and many customers report the fan is surprisingly quiet.

There are a few minor drawbacks: While the storage drawer is roomier than some, it feels quite flimsy. And you’ll need to purchase the air fry tray separately. Still, for the price, it’s hard to beat. For a step up, the brand’s Gallery range has a fifth knob, synchronized burner, and European convection at a slightly higher price point.

Outfit your kitchen on a budget with this freestanding electric range from GE. The no-frills 30-inch model has coil burners and limited features, but it still performs reliably, earning high praise from reviewers.

The stove delivers the power you want and offers decent oven capacity with 5 cubic feet of space. Dual bake elements in the oven provide more-even cooking. There’s also a full-width storage drawer at the bottom. If you just need your electric stove to handle the essentials at a low price point, look no further. It's also available in a white finish.

This LG range is a smart, energy-efficient pick that pairs a two-speed fan with a powerful rear heating element to preheat faster and bake more evenly across multiple racks. A built-in air fry feature can crisp up wings, fries, and veggies with no preheating, and the roomy 6.3-cubic-foot oven can easily accommodate large dishes, including a 20-pound turkey and the sides.

The five-burner cooktop has a 3,200-watt element that take dishes from a rapid boil to a simmer, with flexible 2-in-1 elements to fit everything from a small saucepan to your largest sauté pan. Wi-Fi and the LG ThinQ app let you preheat, adjust, and monitor the oven from your phone, or run it hands-free though Alexa or Google. For instance, you can turn a burner off from the other side of your house. It’s also Energy Star-certified, while cleanup is simple thanks to a 10-minute EasyClean cycle and a coating that helps repel spills and stains.

There is no steam-clean option, and the cooktop lacks a control lockout, so it’s not completely kid-proof. Otherwise, LG’s electric range is a solid smart option that makes cooking (and cleaning) easier.

This GE profile range is a top choice for tech-savvy home cooks looking for a sleek, high-performance stove with cutting-edge features. The slide-in model includes no-preheat air-fry mode and built-in Wi-Fi that lets you control oven functions remotely via the SmartHQ app, compatible with Alexa, Google Assistant, iOS, and Android.

The five-burner cooktop offers versatile heating, and includes a 12-inch/9-inch/6-inch power boil element for rapid heating, plus synchronized burners for large cookware and griddles. Inside, European convection ensures even baking and roasting. The fingerprint-resistant stainless-steel finish keeps it looking pristine outside; a 30-minute steam-clean cycle handles messes inside.

All of these bells and whistles make it a pricier option. And, its glide touch controls, which contribute to the stove’s ultra-modern aesthetic, means that every function is operated via touch—much like swiping on an iPad. If you prefer to use physical knobs, this will not be the best fit.

Built for speed and convenience, this freestanding double oven is a great choice for busy kitchens and home chefs who need flexibility, extra cooking space, and power.

Its five burners include a triple-radiant element that adapts to different cookware sizes while the extra-large European convection double oven—at 6.3 cubic feet, one of the largest in this size—ensures faster, even cooking.

A no-preheat setting lets you cook frozen favorites like pizza and lasagna straight from the freezer, saving time on weeknight meals, and a 50-minute steam-cleaning cycle tackles grime. The only downsides? No Wi-Fi or app support, and surprisingly, no air fry.

While most electric stoves on the market span 30 inches, this sleek freestanding GE model maxes out at just 24 inches across—making it a perfect fit for smaller kitchens. Despite its compact size, it doesn’t skimp on functionality: The front controls are easy to reach, the smooth ceramic glass cooktop wipes clean in seconds, and, thanks to its modular backguard, you can choose to install it with a traditional backguard or flip it down to create a slide-in look.

While there are only four burners, no timer, and a smallish standard (not convection) oven, it’s a stylish, efficient choice for studio apartments, small homes, or anyone cooking for one. It also has a 30-minute steam-clean cycle and a built-in storage drawer that’s deeper than many other stoves on the market. (And if your kitchen can handle a standard-sized stove, GE’s 30-inch free-standing range is a solid, very affordable, choice.)

If you need a stove that’s even more compact than the 24-inch GE, the freestanding 19.5-inch Avanti stove offers serious space efficiency and decent functionality at a very low price. Available in stainless or white, it easily tucks into small kitchens, RVs, and tiny homes. Plus, its retro aesthetic adds a vintage touch.

The four old-school coil burners—three 6-inch and one 8-inch—feature chrome reflector bowls and temperature safety sensors for efficient cooking. While they lack the modern sleekness of a glass cooktop, users report they heat up fast. Inside, the 2.1 cubic feet of oven capacity is roomy enough for one-pan baking and roasting and comes with a broiling pan.

That said, this stove is as basic as it gets. It’s perfect for simple fry-ups and one-pan roasts, but serious home cooks will definitely want more precision and features. If size is your limiting factor, Avanti also makes a more-expensive 19.5-inch glass-top electric stove, which some users say is worth the extra cost, as it provides more even contact with cookware for better heat distribution.

Size can be a significant limiting factor, so measure your stove space first. The standard width for ranges is 30 inches, but if you’re outfitting an apartment kitchen, tiny home, or RV, you’ll want to focus on the few narrower models available.

Next, choose your style: Freestanding stoves have finished sides and back guards, allowing them to stand alone. Slide-in models are designed to sit between cabinets for a seamless look; their stovetops typically sit flush to the back wall, which may require a backsplash update. Drop-in ranges need a custom cabinet base for installation.

Most electric cooktops feature smooth surfaces with heating elements housed beneath tempered glass or ceramic, though traditional coil-style options still exist and tend to be much cheaper. Smooth-top stoves are easier to clean, while coil burners are simpler to replace if one fails.

Standard electric ranges typically come with five burners (four on narrower models). One is often a warming burner, useful for timing multiple dishes. Some models also offer bridge elements—also referred to as "synchronized burners"—which link two burners, handy for griddles or oversized pots. If you frequently boil water, look for one with an express boil burner, designed to heat up faster.

Conventional ovens rely on stationary heating elements—one at the bottom for baking, one at the top for broiling—leading to natural heat rise and possible temperature variations. Standard convection improves on this by adding a fan to circulate hot air for more even cooking. European convection (also called “true” convection) goes a step further, with a third heating element behind the fan for uniform heat distribution across multiple racks.

For everyday cooking, conventional or standard convection works fine. But if you want more precise, even baking and roasting, true convection is worth considering. Be prepared for a slight learning curve if switching to convection, as most recipes are designed for conventional ovens. A good rule of thumb: reduce the temperature by 25°F (e.g., 450°F to 425°F, or 375°F to 350°F), or keep the same temperature but cut the cooking time by about 25 percent. Either way, start checking for doneness earlier than the recipe suggests. A meat thermometer can also help ensure accuracy.

Control panel placement affects both aesthetics and functionality. Backguard controls, found on most freestanding stoves, keep buttons and knobs safely out of reach of children but may be less visually streamlined. Front-control stoves, common in slide-in models, offer a sleek, built-in look and easier access to settings but can be a hazard if you have small kids or frequently lean against the stove while cooking. Many models now include touchscreen controls, which allow for precise adjustments and smart features but may require more care to keep clean.

Many newer electric stoves come with high-tech features designed to make cooking more efficient and hands-free. Wi-Fi-enabled models let you monitor and control your oven remotely via an app—preheating, adjusting temperatures, and setting timers from anywhere. Some even integrate with voice assistants like Alexa or Google Assistant for hands-free commands.

Touchscreen controls and digital displays offer a sleek, modern look, but keep in mind that they can be more finicky than traditional knobs, especially when wet or smudged. If you prefer a more tactile experience, look for models with physical dials or a hybrid control panel.

Some ovens now include built-in air fry functions, which circulate superheated air for crispy, fried-like results without the oil. It’s a great feature for quickly roasting veggies, crisping up frozen snacks, or making healthier versions of fried favorites—no extra countertop appliance needed.

Beyond the sticker price, you’ll want to factor in some extra costs. For one, power cords aren’t usually included in the price, and you can’t reuse your old one. Lowe’s, for example, charges $39.98 to install—which includes a new power cord. Some retailers also charge a separate delivery fee. And, if you’re replacing an existing stove, you should expect to pay around $50 to have your old one hauled away and disposed of. Finally, while most stoves come with a one-year limited warranty (which typically covers manufacturing defects and basic repairs), some retailers offer extended protection plans (for an additional fee) at checkout.

When the glass top of my ancient JennAir electric stove cracked—thanks to a DIY mishap (we stood on it to paint a high part of the kitchen; lesson learned)—I had to find an unplanned replacement. Fortunately, the stovetop still worked, giving me time to explore my options. I visited my local Lowe’s and other reputable retailers to assess everything in person and quickly noticed a difference in selection. Suburban stores only carried standard 30-inch ranges, while city retailers stocked a wider variety, including smaller 24-inch models—something to keep in mind if you’re shopping for a compact space.

I assessed everything: control placement (knobs vs. touchscreen and ease of use), oven heating methods, aesthetics, and extra features like voice control (we’re a household that regularly asks Alexa for help in the kitchen). The models I selected come from trusted brands like GE, Samsung, and Frigidaire, with thousands of positive reviews attesting to their reliability and efficiency. Many are top-sellers across multiple retailers, and some incorporate the latest technology to make cooking faster and more enjoyable. I also chose options across various sizes and price points to fit different spaces and budgets—and included a few solid upgrade picks from the same brands for a slight price increase.

Arabella Bowen is a seasoned product tester who specializes in travel, design, tech, home improvement, and outdoor essentials. She’s reviewed everything from roller bags and cameras to hiking equipment and home decor for outlets such as The Montreal Gazette, Fodor's, AFAR, and US Park Pass. #6253. Forever chemicals are supposed to be unbreakable, but new ‘hunter-killer’ chemistry takes them out

A palladium membrane fed hydrogen from inside breaks the bonds in forever chemicals at room temperature instead of just trapping them.

PFAS “forever chemicals” got their name because almost nothing can break them down. They essentially last forever.

Most water filters only trap toxic forever chemicals without actually destroying them. Once the filter is full, that toxic trash still has to go somewhere.

To fix this, scientists invented a new metal-coated filter that uses hydrogen gas to completely break the chemicals apart.

By swapping out the atoms that make these chemicals so tough, the new filter destroys them at normal room temperature.

In tests, it wiped out over 90 percent of the chemicals, proving we can finally destroy this pollution instead of just moving it from the water to a landfill.

Bruce Rittmann, who directs the Biodesign Swette Center for Environmental Biotechnology at Arizona State University, led the work with Min Long and Jie Cheng.

Colleagues at Rice University, the National University of Singapore and two universities in China also took part. The whole study ran in a glass reactor about a foot (30 centimeters) long.

“PFAS are hard to break down, and normal processes that we use don’t work,” Rittmann said. PFAS is the family’s chemical name, and the chemicals are in water, soil, food and people.

“We all have PFAS in us,” he said. “They stay in the environment. They move up the food chain, and so they’re a big legacy problem.”

PFAS, or forever chemicals, are chains of carbon atoms wrapped in fluorine. The coating is what lets nonstick pans and waterproof jackets shed oil and water, and it’s in firefighting foam too.

“It’s called the strongest bond in organic chemistry,” Rittmann said.

In 2024, the EPA set drinking water limits of 4 parts per trillion for PFOA (perfluorooctanoic acid) and PFOS (perfluorooctanesulfonic acid). Three others, including GenX, got a limit of 10 parts per trillion.

The reactor holds 120 hollow plastic fibers coated with a film of palladium. Hydrogen gas is pumped into the hollow core of each fiber, so it reaches the palladium from underneath while the contaminated water sits against the outside.

Palladium splits hydrogen molecules into single atoms. Some stay on the metal’s surface, and others slip in between the palladium atoms and are stored inside the metal, which swells by about 4 percent as it fills.

The study’s central finding is that the two kinds of hydrogen do different jobs.

“The palladium attracts the PFAS molecule, and the palladium attracts the hydrogen and puts them together,” Rittmann explained.

In control runs, hydrogen without palladium did nothing to PFOA. Palladium without hydrogen took about 30 percent of the PFOA out of the water but released no fluoride, likely because the molecules stuck to the metal without breaking.

Hydrogen on the surface helps the membrane capture a PFAS molecule and hold it flat against the metal. The hydrogen stored inside the metal supplies the energy that swaps a fluorine atom for a hydrogen atom, one bond at a time.

Chains with no fluorine left were among the end products.

The team tested that by feeding hydrogen either through the fiber cores or into the air space above the water. PFOA left the water at about the same rate either way. However, feeding through the fibers doubled the rate at which fluoride was released.

The team also ran a commercial palladium-on-carbon catalyst, which holds stored hydrogen for a shorter time. It removed about 85 percent of the PFOA but freed only 37 percent of the fluorine, compared with 51 percent for the membrane film.

In an interview with Earth.com, Rittmann said the way the gas arrives is what sets this reactor apart. Delivering hydrogen straight to the base of the palladium film creates a highly reactive palladium hydride, and that, he said, is what speeds the reaction up.

In the batch tests, each chemical spent 44 hours in the reactor on its own, in water acidified to pH 4, which is more acidic than tap water.

The longer the carbon chain, the faster the chemical was removed and the more of its fluorine came off. PFNA (perfluorononanoic acid), with nine carbons, lost 59 percent of its fluorine.

In contrast, four-carbon PFBS (perfluorobutane sulfonate) lost 26 percent, while PFOA, PFOS and PFHxS (perfluorohexanesulfonic acid) fell in between.

A longer chain sticks to palladium more strongly, the team’s calculations found, and it carries more of the weaker carbon-fluorine bonds that hydrogen can attack first.

GenX didn’t follow the pattern. It has six carbons but an oxygen atom linking two halves of its chain, and that link made it stick less and resist more. Only 27 percent of its fluorine came off, about the same as PFBS.

For Rittmann, the point of the paper is that the membrane took apart all six regulated forever chemicals, which argues for one mechanism that should work across the family.

He told Earth.com that “more than 20,000 PFAS compounds have been produced, and many more than the six are in use.”

For the long test, the team mixed all six chemicals into one feed at 50 micrograms per liter each and pumped it through the reactor without a break.

Over 58 days the membrane removed between 93 and 99 percent of every compound, and the fluoride in the outflow works out to 83 percent of the fluorine coming off.

Fifty micrograms per liter is also 50,000 parts per trillion, more than 10,000 times the EPA limit for PFOA. In no run did the water reach the drinking-water limits themselves. About 10 percent of the palladium was lost over the run.

“I was not at all surprised that we had good long-term performance,” Rittmann said.

His group has run these reactors for longer than 58 days, he said, and has measured the palladium loss directly and found the rate very low. The catalyst keeps working as long as it is not overloaded with PFAS.

“Palladium is expensive,” Rittmann said. “It’s around $50,000 a kilogram.”

Using less of it was not part of this study, Rittmann said, but finding a way to do so “is one of our prime topics these days.”

One approach he would describe is a biofilm, a layer of bacteria that builds up on the outside of the fibers and holds the palladium particles in place.

With the metal inside that film, the palladium reaction and the bacteria’s own breakdown of the chemicals run side by side. “This makes the overall process notably faster,” he said.

Arizona State also described a role alongside existing treatment. Carbon filters or a conventional membrane would first concentrate the PFAS from a large volume of water into a small waste stream. The palladium membrane would then destroy that stream instead of storing it.

Every feed in this study was mixed in the lab, and the team reports no test on water from a real contaminated site.

Whether the membrane can take forever chemicals from parts per billion down to the parts-per-trillion limits that utilities must meet is still an open question.

The group is now scaling the reactor up for pilot tests through a spin-off company, Metric Water Catalyst.

“If things go well, we may be able to do pilot testing in 2027,” Rittmann said.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6252. REVIEW: Spectrum Optics SkyPilot 127

The smart telescope revolution has grown rapidly over the past few years. Most of these scopes focus primarily on electronic imaging, though, and while amateur astronomers may marvel at the images, they also still enjoy the simple pleasure of looking directly through a telescope.

That’s where the SkyPilot 127 from Spectrum Optics ($999) takes a different approach. Rather than replacing direct observing with a screen-based experience, the SP127 combines a traditional 5-inch (127 millimeters) f/15 Maksutov-Cassegrain telescope with a smart guidance and imaging system.

At first glance, the SP127 looks like a conventional catadioptric with a standard finder on a motorized alt-azimuth mount. But looks can be deceiving.

The secret lies in that “finder.” On closer inspection, it is not a finder at all, but a 2.1-inch (53 mm) f/4 ED refractor outfitted with a digital camera. This second optical tube is the heart of the SP127’s electronically assisted system, serving as both guide scope and imager. The guide scope determines the telescope’s position through plate solving, slews to selected targets, maintains tracking, and captures images. Spectrum Optics also includes the same intelligent camera and 53 mm refractor in its separately sold SPi53 Smart Telescope system.

The camera is built around a Sony IMX662 CMOS color sensor with 2.9-micrometer pixels and a resolution of 1920×1080 pixels. It includes 64 gigabytes of onboard storage.

The MirroSky app, available for iOS and Android, is central to the SP127’s operation. It controls target selection, image capture, live stacking, and display, while the guide scope and camera work together to find objects and produce live-stacked images.

Meanwhile, the Maksutov is dedicated primarily to visual observing. The optical tube weighs approximately 6.5 pounds (2.95 kilograms) and measures 14.6 inches (370 mm) long. A Vixen-style dovetail makes it easy to remove the optical tube from the mount. Total weight for the assembled SP127 is about 26 pounds (11.8 kg).

In addition to the guide scope/imager, the SP127 comes with a 25 mm Plössl eyepiece, a 90° 1¼” star diagonal, a screw-on visual back, an adjustable tripod with steel legs 1.5 inches (3.8 centimeters) in diameter, cables, an AC adapter, and a Bahtinov focusing mask for the guide scope. The camera’s nosepiece is also internally threaded to accept standard 1¼” filters.

In its standard configuration, the included camera photographs through the 53 mm refractor rather than the Maksutov. Although the camera is removable, Spectrum Optics recommends a separate camera for imaging through the Maksutov because its long focal length and narrow field are not well-suited to the included camera’s plate-solving system. That doesn’t mean you have to invest in more equipment, though; I took some very nice shots of the Moon simply by holding my iPhone to the Mak’s 25 mm eyepiece.

The SP127’s hybrid arrangement works well in practice. After the user selects a target in the app, the guide scope directs the mount to the correct location, then tracks the sky. The observer can view the target visually through the Maksutov while the guide scope stacks and displays images via the app. A word of caution, however: Be careful not to shake the instrument when looking through the eyepiece. Even a slight motion will blur the image being photographed.

Like most Maksutov-Cassegrain systems, the SP127 excels at medium and high magnifications. Its 1,900 mm focal length is especially well-suited for observing the Moon, planets, planetary nebulae, and double stars.

Spectrum Optics MirroSky SkyPilot SP127 Primary Optical Tube: 5-inch 127mm Maksutov-Cassegrain Focal Length: 1900mm Length: 14.6 inches (370 mm) Focal Ratio: f/15 Guide Scope Optical Tube: 53mm ED refractor with Sony IMX662 CMOS camera Focal Length: 200mm Focal Ratio: f/4 Assembled Weight: 26 lbs. (11.8 kg) Mount Payload: 9 lbs. (4 kg) Connectivity: built-in Wi-Fi, 2.4 and 5 GHz Camera Storage: 64GB onboard storage Tripod: Full-size adjustable steel-leg tripod Eyepiece: 25mm Plössl Price: $999.99 Contact: Spectrum Optics 2175 S Grand Ave Santa Ana, CA 92705 1-888-879-5143 spectrumoi.com

For this review, I arranged to receive a sample SP127 directly from Spectrum Optics. It arrived securely packed and in perfect condition.

Setup was easy, thanks to the well-illustrated paper manual that came with the scope. After I aligned the guide scope with the Maksutov during the day, as the instructions suggested, the scope was ready to go. I had everything together in under half an hour.

Control is handled entirely through the MirroSky app. To initialize the scope to the sky, the system uses onboard sensors combined with date, time, and location information supplied by the connected smart device. The camera includes dual-band Wi‑Fi capability supporting both 2.4 and 5 gigahertz connections. During use, the app’s interface was straightforward and easy to navigate. Target acquisition was quick and accurate. Chosen objects were always centered in the field of view. The app also provides guided tours and a database containing more than 100,000 stars, solar system members, and deep-sky sights.

Tracking performance was accurate for visual observations and short-exposure imaging. Since the SP127 uses an alt-azimuth mount, field rotation may become evident around the edges with longer exposures.

The SP127 can be powered by eight user-supplied AA batteries in the mount, a suitable external 12-volt power source, or the included AC adapter.

I found that the Maksutov performed very well. Lunar views were well-defined, with crater walls, rilles, and other surface features standing out crisply. I was especially impressed when, in moments of steady seeing, the SP127 detected a few of the craterlets on the floor of Plato. It passed another tough test by resolving Schröter’s Valley, a sinuous rille near craters Aristarchus and Herodotus.

Planetary performance also proved impressive. Multiple cloud bands as well as the Great Red Spot were clearly visible on Jupiter, and shadows cast by Galilean moons could also be seen on the planet’s cloud tops.

Double stars were another strong point, thanks to the long focal length. The Trapezium in the Orion Nebula, for instance, was striking. The included eyepiece did well, but the view really sparkled when I swapped in my own eyepieces with shorter focal lengths.

Throughout it all, I was very impressed with the crispness of the images, showing the high quality of the Maksutov’s optics. Like most catadioptric telescopes, the SP127 focuses by moving the primary mirror. This takes tight manufacturing tolerances to maintain a precise focus without tilting the mirror. I found that alignment stayed spot-on after swapping eyepieces and refocusing the view.

I was equally impressed with the imaging results using the 53 mm guide scope. The app allows you to customize settings, including gain, exposure length, number of frames to capture, and dark frames. After I experimented with the settings, the Orion Nebula appeared in vivid color after only two minutes of exposure, even as it was setting in my light-polluted sky. The Pleiades also recorded beautifully, although not all members squeezed into the guide scope’s approximately 1.6° by 0.9° field. The Horsehead Nebula, the Whirlpool Galaxy, the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules, and more displayed details exceeding what you might expect from such a small aperture, especially after post-processing using apps like PixInsight, GIMP, and Photoshop.

The SkyPilot 127 is one of the most original entries in today’s smart telescope market. For observers who still enjoy looking through an eyepiece but appreciate the convenience of app-driven targeting and imaging, the SP127 offers something genuinely special. In a small but growing group of smart telescopes that combine traditional eyepiece observing with integrated electronic imaging, the SP127’s hybrid design makes it an appealing bridge between conventional astronomy and the smart telescope revolution.

Contributing Editor Phil Harrington received the Walter Scott Houston Award in 2018 for his lifelong work in astronomy.

#6251. One day of fatty food was enough to trigger a surprising response in the mouse brain

A high-fat diet changed brain cells involved in eating and weight control within a single day in male mice, revealing an unexpected early response.

Weeks of fatty food are known to blunt a group of brain cells in mice that hold back eating. That reduced activity may contribute to further overeating and weight gain.

Earlier studies measured the cells after at least two weeks on a high-fat diet, leaving their initial response unclear.

Yi Lu and Mark Rossi at Rutgers University examined that initial response and found a different pattern.

After a single day of high-fat food, the cells in male mice fired more easily than before, which the authors read as the brain trying to limit weight gain.

In female mice, the same cells already fired easily on a normal diet, and the fatty food didn’t change that.

The cells are in the lateral hypothalamus, a region near the base of the brain that helps control eating and has been studied as a feeding center since the 1950s.

Rossi is an assistant professor at Robert Wood Johnson Medical School and a resident scientist at the Child Health Institute of New Jersey.

He has spent years on one group of those cells, the ones that release the signaling chemical glutamate. Switching those cells on makes a mouse eat less, so the team calls them a brake.

Lu recorded from single cells in thin slices of mouse brain, using a glass pipette fine enough to seal onto one neuron and read its electrical activity.

Pushing a small current into each cell showed how readily it fired.

On a normal diet, the brake cells in females fired more times for the same push than the cells in males did. Their electrical spikes were also narrower.

Female cells also received inhibitory signals from neighboring cells more often, so they were both easier to fire and more often held back.

The baseline recordings came from 40 cells in three male mice and 51 cells in three female mice.

The team also recorded cells from other mice after one, two, or seven days on a high-fat diet.

Fat supplied 60% of the calories in the experimental diet, compared with 21% in the mice’s usual chow.

In males, one day was enough. The brake cells fired more for the same current, and they needed less current to fire at all. The change was there on day one, day two, and day seven.

In females, the firing rate was unchanged at the one-, two-, and seven-day measurements.

The team wrote that the male result surprised them, since the two-week studies had pointed the other way.

The signals arriving at the cells shifted too, but not in the same direction. In males, the excitatory inputs that drive these cells grew less frequent.

In females, it was the inhibitory inputs that dropped, and only briefly: by day seven they were back to normal.

The input recordings came from just two mice per group, which the authors list as a limit on what they can say about them.

A cell that fires more easily on fatty food could be part of the problem or part of the body’s defense.

To tell which, the team gave the brake cells a bacterial sodium channel called NaChBac, which keeps them in a more excitable state. Then they weighed the mice every day for a week.

Male mice with the extra excitability gained less weight than control males, on normal chow and on the fatty diet alike.

Female mice on chow were unaffected, which the authors think fits with their cells already being excitable. Female mice on the fatty diet lost weight.

The treated mice weren’t eating less. Over six hours with the fatty food in front of them, treated mice of both sexes ate more of it.

Their activity in an open arena didn’t change either.

The authors wrote that the weight difference most likely comes from the mice burning more energy, though they didn’t measure that directly.

Female mice tend to put on weight more slowly than males on a high-fat diet, and the authors see the brake cells as one reason why.

In males, the quick response may hold off some weight gain before the longer-term blunting sets in.

Raising the cells’ excitability, the authors wrote, may limit weight gain without reducing food intake.

Everything here happened in mice, and in a region of the brain where many kinds of cells are mixed together.

The recordings couldn’t separate the subtypes of brake cells, so the team can’t say which ones changed.

Nor can they say whether the shift in incoming signals came from the cells sending them or from the connections themselves.

Why the female cells start out more excitable is also open. Males and females often respond differently to fasting and overfeeding, and removing the ovaries from female mice makes them gain weight the way males on fatty food do.

The authors expect estrogen to be involved, but this study tested no hormone.

The biggest open question is how a brake that fires more easily on day one ends up blunted by week two.

The team suspects the cells recalibrate under sustained pressure, the way neurons across the brain adjust to a lasting change in their input.

No one has yet recorded the same cells across that whole stretch. The authors wrote that a study following them from the first day to the second week is what it would take.

The full study was published in the journal The Journal of Neuroscience.

A genetic analysis has identified two previously unrecognized species of howler monkey that change these primates' evolutionary tree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have identified two newfound species of howler monkey in the Amazon rainforest. The discoveries could redraw branches of these primates' evolutionary tree, a new study shows.

The new species were named Alouatta iroi and Alouatta matogrossensis. The adorable creatures have bushy beards, winsome expressions and bright red fur. Their identification raises the number of known howler monkey species to 16, researchers said in a statement.

"Our study shows that the Amazon still holds remarkable biological secrets, even among well-known animals such as howler monkeys," study first author Romina Batista, a biodiversity scientist at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

One of the newfound species, A. matogrossensis, is probably on the brink of extinction. The other newfound species faces threats from a planned dam on the Rio Branco River, according to the study.

In addition to identifying the new species, the study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Communications Biology, used genetic evidence to understand when howler monkeys spread out and diversified. The researchers analyzed the genomes of 11 howler monkey species living in South and Central America, combining existing DNA datasets with new genomic information from specimens in Brazilian zoological collections.

The newfound howler monkey species Alouatta iroi, photographed in Guiana.

Overall, the genetic data confirmed that howler monkeys diverged from close relatives between 19 million and 13.5 million years ago. But the analysis changed the picture of more recent evolution.

For instance, the team argued that the Tapajós red-handed howler (A. tapajozensis) and the Amazonian black howler (A. nigerrima) are not as closely related as scientists previously thought. The researchers also said that the Trinidad howler (A. insulanus), whose status has been unclear, should be confirmed as a separate species.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"This discovery comes at a critical time, as increasing deforestation, climate change and habitat loss threaten many Amazonian species before they are fully understood or even discovered by science," study co-author Jean Boubli, a professor and chair of primate ecology and evolution at the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

The scientists found that natural barriers such as the Amazon River, the Xingu River and the Branco River drove many howler monkeys to develop separately. Researchers believe that howler monkeys can swim across small waterways, but big rivers block groups from mixing, which led to different traits and species evolving over time. Natural barriers are a common reason why species emerge in the Amazon, the researchers noted in the study.

#6249. A tube made of tiny speakers is called ‘the closest thing to magic’ this scientist has ever seen

Finnish physicists turned ultrasound into a sound tube with no walls that steers water, powder, gas and even sparks along bendable paths.

Making water flow horizontally through the air without spilling sounds like magic. But scientists in Finland just made it happen by inventing a brand new kind of pipe.

Instead of using plastic or metal, they built an invisible tube out of sound waves that holds a stream of liquid perfectly in mid-air.

Ari Salmi and Dmitry Nikolaev of the University of Helsinki built the device with colleagues at the Public University of Navarre in Spain and the University of Michigan.

A ring of 256 small ultrasonic speakers, each about the size of a shirt button, surrounds the water from about 2 inches (5 centimeters) away. They push on it from every side, but a person standing next to the ring doesn’t hear a thing.

“Of all the experimental setups I have seen, I would say this is the closest thing to magic,” said Salmi, a professor of electronics who led the development of the device.

The same ring, driven differently, guided powder, mist, two heavy gases and even an electric spark along paths the team could bend on command. So far it works over a stretch about 3 inches (8 centimeters) long.

Sound is pressure moving through air. A loud enough sound pushes on whatever it meets. Labs have used that push for decades to float a drop of water or a small bead in mid-air.

Levitation of that kind moves one object, or a few, at a time. Alternatively, it needs a solid vibrating surface underneath. A wall-free channel that carries a flowing stream and bends on command is the new part.

The Helsinki team worked out how to time the 256 speakers so that their waves add up into a long, thin field. Its strongest pressure wraps around a quiet core, like the walls of a hose. Anything inside gets pushed back toward the center whenever it drifts.

Change the timing and the field bends. The team sent the water straight through the sound tube, then tilted it left and right. They shifted where the water landed by about six-tenths of an inch (16 millimeters) without losing a drop.

Salmi, answering questions from Earth.com together with Nikolaev, said the thing that surprised them most was simple. “We were surprised that the ultrasonic pipe does not leak,” he said.

The sound tube has settings, and different forms of matter need different settings. A field shaped like a long donut, with high pressure around a hollow center, held a stream of water in place.

It also held single drops about a sixteenth of an inch (1 to 2 millimeters) across.

The donut field failed on fine powder, though. Grains of silica about the width of a human hair started circling inside it. They were caught in a slow swirl of air that the sound itself stirs up. The swirl flung them out.

A field with petal-shaped lobes around the center kept the powder on track instead. Only a few stray grains fell along the way.

Gases needed a third setting, with the pressure focused down the middle.

Carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide, both heavier than air, followed the field in a hollow sheath around that core. So did the mist from a household humidifier. Helium, which is lighter than air, couldn’t be steered at all in these tests.

“By changing how the speakers are controlled, we can reshape and turn the tube as needed,” said Nikolaev, a postdoctoral researcher who led the team on the project.

“Transporting a solid substance, for example, requires a different field configuration than transporting a liquid or a gas.”

The strangest passenger in the sound tube was a spark. The team put the tip of a small Tesla coil inside it. With the sound off, its discharge jumped in random directions and wandered as much as an inch (25 millimeters) from side to side.

With the sound on, the spark locked onto the path that the field traced. It strayed by only about a millimeter, roughly the width of the glowing channel itself.

A spark heats a thin thread of air, and the authors argue that the same sound pressure that steers a gas steers that thread.

The team used the steered spark to weld the edges of two plastic pieces without touching them.

Other demonstrations in the paper spelled the letter E in water drops on a plate and filled rows of tiny wells with liquid or powder. One merged two liquid streams in mid-air.

The tricks point at 3D printing. Powder came through the ring at about a seventh of an ounce (4.2 grams) a minute, near the low end of what metal printers feed. Liquid came through at up to 1 fluid ounce (30 milliliters) a minute, more than most printers that lay down living cells push.

The ring runs at about 40,000 vibrations a second, too high-pitched for a human ear to register. The pressure inside isn’t gentle.

“At the core of the device, the intensity of the ultrasound is comparable to a continuous roar of gunfire right next to your ear,” Nikolaev said. “But it is too high-pitched for the human ear.”

Salmi said the idea came to him on an evening dog walk four years ago. His lab had built a device that cleaned the insides of pipes with ultrasound. At lunch, a colleague had remarked that it would be handy if a pipe had no surface for dirt to stick to.

The University of Helsinki has filed a patent application on the method, naming Salmi and Nikolaev among the inventors.

The prototype is a tabletop device. In their answers to Earth.com, Salmi and Nikolaev said it’s meant for small, delicate flows rather than anything resembling plumbing.

They expect the stream’s width can grow to about an eighth to a fifth of an inch (3 to 5 millimeters).

The field is also easily disturbed. Any turbulence in a gas stream broke the guidance. The researchers had to drape fabric around the device to block drafts in the room.

Sound bouncing around inside the cylinder weakened the field more than their calculations predicted, which is one reason they built the steering section as a widening cone.

The first real jobs, the two researchers told Earth.com, will likely be moving gases, “since there are very few current methods that can do that.”

They added, “We find the universality of the method very intriguing – it works with all states of matter (solids, liquids, gases and plasma).”

Whether chained modules can carry a stream across a bench, or a room, is the question a 3-inch prototype can’t answer. The team’s code for shaping the fields is public, so other labs with speaker arrays can now try.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6248. Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Asteroid defense is the mission’s top priority, but there’s also fascinating science to be done.

The Hera spacecraft’s Asteroid Framing Camera captured this black-and-white image of Didymos and Dimorphos from about 60 kilometers away. The photo shows the far side of Didymos compared to the DART impact.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

Didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”

DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.)

Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

Scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” says planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” says planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always showed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” says planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

Similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

#6246. How to watch Starship Flight 15

SpaceX is set to launch its 15th test flight of Starship on Friday, Nov. 13. For the first time, the company will try to catch both stages of the rocket — the Super Heavy booster and the upper stage, which SpaceX calls “Ship” — with the arms of its launch tower. If it works, Starship will become the first orbital rocket ever recovered in full.

SpaceX is targeting a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (4:45 p.m. CST) Friday from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas, pending regulatory approval. Starship launch dates often slip, so check the company’s Flight 15 mission page for the latest.

SpaceX’s live webcast begins about 30 minutes before liftoff — around 5:15 p.m. EST if the launch holds at the start of the window. You can stream it on the Flight 15 mission page or on SpaceX’s X account.

If you’re near the Texas-Mexico border, crowds typically gather on South Padre Island, across the bay from the launch site. On the Mexican side, the public beach at Playa Bagdad offers a head-on view of the launch tower.

About six and a half minutes after liftoff, Super Heavy should fly back to Starbase and be plucked from the air by the tower’s “chopstick” arms, a catch SpaceX has made three times before. Ship will continue to orbit and release 26 of SpaceX’s next-generation Starlink V3 satellites.

The real test comes the next day. Ship will circle Earth about 14 times at roughly 171 miles (275 kilometers) up before heading home. Until now, Ship’s test flights have ended with a practice landing at sea: it flips upright, and then fires its engines to set down gently on the water. This time, it will run that same maneuver over Starbase and hopefully settle into the tower’s arms instead. SpaceX’s flight timeline puts the catch about 22 and a half hours after launch — around 4:18 p.m. EST on Saturday, Nov. 14, if Starship lifts off on time.

SpaceX says Ship will head for the tower only if flight controllers confirm that every system it needs for reentry, the landing burn, and the final approach is healthy. If not, the company can bring Ship down at preplanned spots in the Pacific, with go/no-go checks built into the flight for splashdowns near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile.

#6245. Climate change is unfolding very differently just inches above the ground

Microclimate research finds climate change can warm one slope while cooling another nearby, and most wildlife lives in that near-ground air.

Climate change usually arrives as one number for a whole region: so many degrees warmer than it used to be.

A regional average may reveal little about the conditions a beetle, seedling or toad experiences near the ground.

New research finds that air near the ground can warm much faster than the regional average, barely at all, or even cool while the region heats up.

The clearest example in the review is a patch of coast in southwest England about 1.2 miles (2 kilometers) on a side.

A computer reconstruction of its hottest days from 1983 to 2015 put the regional warming at about half a degree Fahrenheit (0.3°C). Inside that patch, one spot warmed by 5.2°F (2.9°C) and another cooled by 2.3°F (1.3°C).

Same coast, same three decades, opposite directions.

Caroline Greiser, a researcher at Stockholm University and its Bolin Centre for Climate Research, led the review with 20 colleagues from Europe, South Africa and the United States.

They call this near-ground climate the microclimate, and it doesn’t change at the same rate as the climate around it.

“Climate change is often described as a single number for a region. But organisms live in specific places – in a particular patch of forest or on a particular slope. The climate they experience can change at a very different rate from the regional average,” Greiser said.

The regional number comes from weather stations, which are deliberately placed in open spots away from trees and slopes.

It also comes from climate models that work on grid squares 6 to 60 miles (10 to 100 kilometers) across. Neither can see the shade under a shrub.

The review doesn’t report new field measurements.

It pulls together published work from atmospheric science and ecology and adds three computer simulations of real landscapes, run with models built by Ilya Maclean of the University of Exeter.

The simulations track the air 2 inches (5 centimeters) above the ground, where many small land animals and seedlings live.

The physics is simple to state. Sunlight that reaches the ground either warms the surface and the air above it, evaporates water, or gets stored in soil and plants.

Anything that shifts that split shifts the temperature a small creature feels.

A 2022 study found that daytime cloud cover over Europe fell by roughly 1.5% to 2% between the periods 1980 to 1995 and 2000 to 2015.

Extra sun on a clear day lands far harder on a south-facing slope than on a forest floor, so an uneven landscape gets more uneven as the clouds thin out.

At night, clouds catch heat rising off the ground and send part of it back down, which can keep near-ground temperatures warmer than on a clear night.

On a clear, calm night, cold air drains downhill and collects in hollows, and a valley bottom can frost while the slope above it doesn’t.

The team’s simulation of a landscape in the Spanish Pyrenees put numbers on this.

Doubling the cloud cover instead of halving it lowered near-ground temperatures on the hottest days of the year by about 22°F (12.4°C) on average, with the strongest cooling on open ground.

The same change in the sky cooled some patches far more than others.

Snow mattered most on the coldest nights. A snow blanket raised minimum near-ground temperatures by about 5.4°F (3°C) on average, roughly ten times the effect of wind or air humidity.

Where winter snow is disappearing, that insulation goes with it.

Warming is pushing shrubs and trees into grasslands and tundra in many parts of the world.

The review’s third simulation took a 0.4-square-mile (1-square-kilometer) patch of the Anatolian steppe in Turkey and filled it in with the shrubs and trees growing at a nearby site.

On the hottest days of the year, near-ground temperatures fell by up to 30°F (16.6°C) under tall, dense shrubs and trees, while open patches where the model made the grass shorter warmed by up to 11°F (6°C).

The same landscape, under the same sky, went two directions at once.

“Vegetation is not simply responding to climate change – it can also modify the climate experienced by organisms living under canopies,” Greiser said.

“When vegetation changes, it changes the local energy balance, and this can lead to very different temperature trends within the same landscape.”

Smaller shifts are already under way. In a mixed forest in New Hampshire, spring leaves came out earlier between 1982 and 2019.

The review’s second simulation found that the extra April leaf cover changed the forest floor’s minimum and maximum temperatures by only about a third of a degree Fahrenheit (0.2°C) each.

The shade can also vanish fast. Droughts, insect outbreaks, fires and storms strip canopies, and a single disturbance can expose a forest floor to conditions equal to several decades of regional warming at once.

Earth.com has reported the same pattern after bark beetle outbreaks and in fragmented forests.

Which plants take over matters too. In a large tree-planting experiment in China, plots with 24 tree species grew denser canopies than single-species plots, and the ground beneath them was up to 7.9°F (4.4°C) cooler.

In the Arctic, shrubs replacing pale lichen can reflect only half as much sunlight, because dark vegetation absorbs far more than lichen or snow.

Jonas Lembrechts of the University of Antwerp is a senior author on the review.

He and his co-authors point to the growing number of long-term near-ground temperature records as the way to check simulations like these against measurements taken on the ground.

Cool pockets, such as forested slopes and basins where cold air pools, might warm more slowly than the open ground beside them. The review finds the evidence for that mixed.

Forty-five years of records from a forested mountain watershed showed little difference in long-term warming between sites, despite frequent cold-air pooling.

Across Austria, by contrast, winter temperature inversions became 11% less frequent between 1961 and 2017, and low-lying sites warmed faster as a result.

The mixed evidence is the practical problem. Predictions of where species can live are mostly built from regional climate data.

The authors argue those predictions will keep misjudging which populations are safe until they account for what happens at ground level.

“If we want to understand where species will persist and where they will be most vulnerable, we need to know not only how the regional climate is changing, but also how that change translates into the microclimates organisms actually experience,” Greiser said.

The simulations changed one thing at a time, clouds or wind or snow, while holding everything else steady.

Real weather changes several of them at once, so the team describes the runs as illustrations of single mechanisms rather than forecasts.

The landscape model also leaves out cold air draining downhill, so real patterns are probably patchier than the maps show.

The review also deals mostly in averages, which the authors wrote can hide the heat waves and frosts that actually push a species out of a place.

The hardest open problem they name is physical.

How heat and moisture move through a tangle of branches and leaves is still hard to quantify, so how strongly vegetation shields or amplifies warming remains uncertain.

Long-term records that track vegetation and near-ground temperature together, in the same places, are what would settle it. Those paired records remain rare.

“The processes that determine microclimate are complex and involve both atmospheric and biological systems. Understanding them therefore requires collaboration between atmospheric scientists and ecologists,” Greiser said.

The full study was published in the journal Global Change Biology.

The Pan American Health Organization has determined that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, meaning domestic spread of the virus is now significant and sustained.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Measles is officially back in the United States after the disease had been eliminated from the country for more than 25 years.

The U.S. officially eliminated measles in 2000, meaning that at that time, the country had gone over a year without continuous domestic spread of the disease. Travelers would occasionally bring measles into the country, sometimes sparking significant local outbreaks, but these didn't tip enough dominoes to lead to ongoing domestic transmission.

That status has now changed, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday (Nov. 13). The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is the regional office of the World Health Organization for the Americas, has reevaluated the United States' measles elimination status and determined that it should be revoked. With this decision, the U.S. joins several other nations that have seen a local return of measles, including the U.K. and Canada.

The decision follows a series of major measles outbreaks that kicked off in January 2025. Nearly 2,300 cases were reported nationwide in 2025, and so far in 2026, almost 5,412 confirmed cases have been confirmed, although both tallies are likely undercounts.

"When January 2025 picked up, I felt like this might be the point of no return," Maimuna Majumder, a distinguished scholar in the Computational Health Informatics Program at Boston Children's Hospital, previously told Live Science. "I do want to just stress that measles elimination has always been a tenuous prospect, and it is, by design, tenuous," she added.

It takes work to keep an eliminated disease from resurging. The effort rests largely on keeping vaccination rates above a critical threshold — because the measles virus spreads so easily, at least 95% of the population needs immunity via either vaccination or past infection to prevent large outbreaks from occurring and fueling uncontrolled spread. National measles vaccination rates have been falling in recent years, with just 10 states reporting rates above the immunity threshold among kindergarteners for 2025-2026.

Experts point to several factors to explain the trend, including declining funds and staff for public health efforts and wavering public trust in vaccines and scientific expertise. The appointment of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary and the loss of long-standing federal health leadership further fueled the trend, they say, as vaccine guidance has been changed in ways that likely sow confusion and the federal rhetoric around vaccines now frames their safety and effectiveness as open questions when they are actually well-established.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Measles infections can have serious consequences, including long-term disability and death.

The nation's first measles-related deaths this year were reported in Pennsylvania in August, and five more have followed, according to state health officials. (Some of these deaths have not been confirmed by the federal government.) A death reported in Wisconsin and another in New York have brought the current total to eight, per states' counts.

In the U.S., about 1 to 3 out of every 1,000 measles cases results in death. Pennsylvania has recorded just over 1,500 cases, so its number of reported deaths is higher than expected, hinting that the state's true case rate has not been fully captured in the data.

In survivors, measles can cause long-term health problems, including brain damage and immune amnesia, in which the immune cells tasked with remembering past infections have their "memories" wiped.

The PAHO's meeting to reevaluate the United States' status was originally scheduled for April but was pushed to November.

To regain its measles elimination status, the U.S. must go 12 months without continuous spread of the virus.

#6243. An excavator found figurine molds at a Sudan temple in 1912 that was once a faience workshop

Digs at Sanam Temple in Sudan from 2018 to 2020 found a workshop from the mid-600s BC that made green figurines for Kush's royal tombs.

In 1912 the Egyptologist Francis Llewellyn Griffith dug at Sanam Temple, on the Nile in northern Sudan. His single season there lasted three months. He removed the fill on a light narrow-gauge Decauville railway.

Griffith also found clay molds for shabtis, the little figurines put in tombs. In 1922, however, he wrote only that they revealed one of the industries pursued in the temple.

He did not go looking for the place where that industry worked. Griffith did not systematically explore outside the walls, and he dumped his spoil heaps right up against them.

Excavations from 2018 to 2020 have now uncovered the faience workshop, behind the temple’s rear wall. It had three firing pits, two mudbrick basins and hundreds of beads, and it dates to the mid-seventh century BC. Some of its raw materials are still not identified with certainty.

King Taharqo ruled Kush and Egypt from about 690 to 664 BC. He founded the temple around 675 BC at Napata, his capital near the Fourth Cataract. He dedicated it to Amun-Bull-of-Nubia, a local form of the god.

A building known as the royal treasury stood nearby and held imported storage jars, finished goods and elephant tusks. The town grew up near Jebel Barkal, on land where shifts in the Nile created stable ground for a city.

Taharqo built all the way from the Nile delta to Napata. Much of his effort went to Karnak, where the oldest part of the temple sat on high ground among Nile channels. On the walls at Sanam is the Sanam Historical Inscription, the longest Kushite royal inscription that survives.

The new project’s first season lasted three weeks in January 2018. Kathryn Howley of New York University’s Institute of Fine Arts wrote it up in the first field report.

It also lists two rifle cartridges, probably from the late 19th century, by a wall the team suspects was Kitchener’s Fort, a colonial building Griffith took down.

Trench 3 was opened to the rear of the temple as a square of about 8 feet (2.5 meters). Below a lot of charcoal came faience beads, one intricately molded piece and wasters, lumps that went wrong in the firing.

Small shells and grinding stones lay with them. Workmen also picked up many beads on the surface around Griffith’s old spoil heaps.

In 2019 and 2020, workers from Karima and Merawi helped widen the trench to about 16 feet (5 meters) a side. Under the pits, the team then found a floor of broken storage jars. Someone had laid them flat to give a solid surface to work on.

The ash around the pits held hundreds of disk beads in blue, green and white, plus bits of faience vessels. Faience is mostly silica, with some alkali and lime. Simple ovens can reach the roughly 1,650 degrees Fahrenheit (900 degrees Celsius) needed to fire it.

One fragment, a broken green shabti, had no inscription on it. A new clay mold found inside the temple matches it exactly. Griffith’s older molds match shabtis George Reisner dug up at Nuri, the royal cemetery.

In Napatan Nubia only royalty used shabtis, while in Egypt people of many ranks had them. Egyptian cliff tombs still turn up burial goods, such as the pottery vessels and mirrors in rock-cut tombs of the south.

The paper calls Sanam “the first workshop securely identified for Kushite Nubia.” Egyptian marl jars with folded rims under the floor point to the eighth and seventh centuries BC. Red-slipped beakers fit the same range.

Faience paste needs lime. In Egypt it probably came from limestone, but most of Sudanese Nubia sits on the Nubian sandstone formation and has very little of it.

In 2018 Howley took the shells for Nile snails, which would have been easy to collect. She also noted that they were too small for anyone to gather just for food.

The new paper is by Rennan Lemos of Durham University’s Department of Archaeology, Howley and independent scholar Siobhan Shinn. Shadia Abdu Rabo of Sudan’s National Corporation for Antiquities and Museums co-wrote it.

The shells came out of the ash by the thousands. One bivalve is most likely Transkeia globosa, a Red Sea clam once called Diplodonta globosa.

Some snail shells still show traces of brown, and their shape fits both Nile snails of the family Hydrobiidae and marine Phasianellidae.

Workers broke the shells in the mudbrick basins with grindstones, which still carry the marks. Then they mixed the powder into the paste before firing.

Earlier Nubian potters had also put shell into their clay. Hauling so much shell from the coast was no small task. The authors argued that it took either direct control of distant communities or deals with desert groups who moved goods.

They described the shell-based recipe as a locally adapted version of an Egyptian craft. They also argued it served the production of objects for royal use.

Faience firing gives off smoke, and the smell depends on the fuel. In Egypt, workshops often made faience at the edge of a settlement, where the wind took the fumes off.

At Sanam, however, workers dug the pits immediately outside the temple’s sandstone wall. The authors read that placement as a sign that the temple controlled production, with some items meant only for royal use.

The 2020 season also turned up dark resin nuggets wedged between flagstones in the rear rooms. The team burned one lump as an experiment. It gave off a heavy, sweet smell like the bakhuur incense used in Sudan today, Howley wrote in her 2019-2020 report.

Shape alone could not settle the snail species. But the ongoing war in Sudan, the authors wrote, prevents further analysis. A mixed batch of Nile and Red Sea shells is still possible.

Nobody knows yet if real kilns stood over the pits. Collapsed mudbrick between pits 1 and 2 might be kiln walls. Then again, the workers might have used a cover they could lift off. The team dated the workshop by its pottery, and the paper gives no radiocarbon dates.

The authors think household workshops also made beads and pendants for ordinary people. Faience, after all, turns up in Sanam’s large non-elite cemetery. However, no one has yet fully investigated those other recipes with scientific methods.

New York University’s Institute of Fine Arts and the Egypt Exploration Society funded the fieldwork. An Explorers Club Rolex Grant and the Shelby White and Leon Levy Program paid too. Sudan’s antiquities corporation gave permission for the work, with help from its inspector, el-Hassan Ahmed.

Griffith wrote about his molds in 1922 without knowing where anyone had used them. Now, in Trench 3, the team has found the pits and the beads. It has also found a green shabti that fits a mold from inside the temple.

The full study was published in the journal Antiquity.

#6242. Air pollution’s link to blood sugar has a surprising temperature twist

A European study links air pollution and temperature swings to higher blood sugar, offering clues to how environmental conditions may interact.

Air pollution is usually discussed as a threat to the lungs, while heat is treated as a seasonal health risk.

In a study of more than 21,000 Europeans without diabetes, particle pollution and temperature variability were linked to higher long-term blood sugar. The association with each depended on exposure to the other.

In modeled scenarios, reducing air pollution was associated with a larger drop in blood sugar under warmer, more variable conditions.

The study found no measurable association between residential greenery and blood sugar.

Nicole Probst-Hensch and her colleagues at the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute and the University of Basel led the work.

Each person was measured once or a few times. So the study can show that pollution, temperature and blood sugar go together, not that one causes the other.

The team pooled nine long-running studies from Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain, the Czech Republic, Germany and Switzerland.

Together, they held 33,989 blood samples from 21,259 people, drawn between 1999 and 2021.

Ages ran from eight-year-olds in a Dutch birth cohort to the oldest adults in a Stockholm study.

The largest single group was 5,464 people from the GCAT study at the Germans Trias i Pujol Research Institute (IGTP) near Barcelona.

Each blood sample was tested for glycated hemoglobin, or HbA1c, which reflects average blood sugar over the previous two to three months.

Anyone with a diabetes diagnosis, diabetes medication or a reading in the diabetic range was left out, allowing the researchers to examine environmental associations in people without diabetes.

Each home address was then matched to a year of air pollution, greenery and temperature, from Europe-wide maps built by the EXPANSE project.

Of the three pollutants on the maps, only PM10 showed a consistent link to higher blood sugar.

PM10 includes airborne particles up to 10 micrometers across, including both fine and coarser particles. Nitrogen dioxide showed no consistent association, while the link with the finer PM2.5 was less consistent.

The other signal was how much the daily temperature swung over a year, more than the average temperature itself.

Their statistical method was built to find exposures that act together, and it did. Coarse particles and temperature swings interacted, so the effect of one depended on the level of the other.

The temperature-swing terms held up in nine of ten rounds of re-testing on different slices of the data.

One interaction, fine particles with average temperature, did not, and the authors treat it with caution.

Why would coarse particles matter for blood sugar? Larger particles get trapped in the upper airways, are moved up to the mouth and are swallowed, the authors wrote.

That fits other studies suggesting air pollution may alter gut bacteria.

The team then ran three futures through its model. The first cut coarse particles and nitrogen dioxide by 10 micrograms per cubic meter of air, and fine particles by 5.

These reductions were intended to approximate progress toward World Health Organization guideline levels. In the model, they were associated with lower blood sugar.

The second scenario raised the yearly average temperature by 0.9°F (0.5°C) and widened daily temperature swings by 1.8°F (1°C). The model associated these changes with higher blood sugar.

The third scenario combined cleaner air with warmer, more variable temperatures. Together, these changes were associated with a larger decrease in blood sugar than cleaner air alone.

The researchers expressed these modeled changes in standard deviations, a measure of how much blood sugar varied across the group.

Cleaner air alone was associated with a decrease of about 0.06 standard deviations, compared with about 0.07 under the combined scenario.

That is small for any one person. But most future diabetes comes from the many people at low or moderate risk, the authors wrote, so a small shift across a population matters.

The pattern was stronger in the 28,089 samples from nonsmokers and absent in the 5,900 from smokers.

Smoking causes inflammation of its own, the authors wrote, which may mask the effect.

Trees and parks are the usual prescription for a hot, polluted city. The study measured greenness around each home from satellite images, and the distance to the nearest green space.

Neither was linked to blood sugar, on its own or in combination with pollution or heat.

The links between pollution, temperature variability and blood sugar appeared almost exclusively in cities. In the less urban half of the samples, no stable link appeared.

The authors put that down to higher pollution and stronger heat islands in urban areas.

Natàlia Blay, a postdoctoral researcher at GCAT and a co-author, put the result in a wider frame.

“Including temperature in this approach is particularly relevant in the current context of climate change, where environmental exposures cannot be understood in isolation,” she said.

Diet and physical activity were not included in the models.

Participants had blood sugar measured once or a few times, so the study could not establish whether pollution caused higher blood sugar or whether other differences between people explained the association.

When the team split the group by body weight, the links disappeared in both halves.

The authors suggested that body fat might help explain the association, although this analysis could not establish its role.

The temperature maps began in 2003, so earlier blood samples were matched to later weather. HbA1c reflects only the three months before a blood draw, while the exposures were yearly averages.

Traffic noise, which other studies have tied to diabetes, had no Europe-wide map and was left out.

Whether cleaning the air of a hot city lowers its diabetes rate is the question the scenarios point at but can’t answer.

The authors wrote that noise belongs in the next round of this work, once Europe-wide noise maps exist.

The full study was published in the journal Environment International.
